subject: Genetics
title: Finishing the Last Gaps
description: A quick, practical guide to Finishing the Last Gaps.

hook.text: The genome was 'complete' in 2003. But 8% was missing—gaps nobody could read. It took 19 more years to finish.

buildup.text: Centromeres and telomeres—chromosome centers and tips—contain extreme repeats that old technology couldn't read.

discovery.text: In 2022, the T2T consortium filled every gap. Nanopore sequencing read ultra-long fragments, solving the puzzle.

twist.text: The missing 8% contained nearly 2,000 new genes. What we'd ignored for 19 years turned out to be important.

climax.text: The truly complete genome was published in 2022—32 years after the project began. Science moves in decades.

punchline.text: The last 8% took longer than the first 92%.

quiz.question: When was the truly complete human genome finally published?
